title: Prepare a Salesforce Portfolio for Review
summary: Make one project easy for another developer to understand, run and assess.
prerequisites: A completed Salesforce exercise or project.
Basic Git and repository skills from the Junior path.
learningObjectives: Explain the project before the folders.
Demonstrate a decision and its limits.

sections.heading: A portfolio is a reviewable explanation
body: A repository full of metadata is not yet an effective portfolio. A reviewer needs to know what the project does, which part you built, how to try it and what its limitations are. Start with one project you understand well. The Northstar test-drive application is suitable because it connects a visible user workflow to data, automation and tests.

Label it as a training project and describe its fictional business context. Explain who uses the feature: a salesperson records a customer’s test-drive request. The customer is represented by a Contact record and does not automatically have a Salesforce login. This small detail demonstrates that you understand the user and data model rather than only the code.

callouts.text: Make the reviewer’s first five minutes useful: purpose, demonstration, setup and evidence.

sections.heading: Write a README that answers practical questions
body: Begin with a short problem statement and a screenshot or brief recorded demonstration. Then explain the main objects and the flow of one successful request. Add prerequisites, installation commands that you have actually checked, the test command and the expected result. If a feature requires an Agentforce-enabled org or a separate product, say so before the setup steps.

Include a short design decision section. For example, explain why Test_Drive__c uses lookups and how that affects its access model. A decision is stronger when it includes a trade-off, not just a claim of best practice. Add known limitations such as mock availability or the absence of a real calendar integration. These help a reviewer distinguish the implemented scope from future ideas.

codeBlocks.caption: Reusable working prompt or template
codeBlocks.code:
# Northstar Test-Drive Training Project

## Problem and users
## Short demonstration
## What I implemented
## Data model and request flow
## Prerequisites and setup
## Tests and observed results
## Design decisions
## Known limitations
## Next improvements

sections.heading: Keep the repository safe and reproducible
body: Before making a project public, inspect the files you are about to publish. Exclude authentication state, private keys, local configuration containing secrets and real customer data. Use synthetic records for demonstrations. The SAM starter already excludes common Salesforce authentication directories, but an ignore file cannot remove a secret that was previously committed.

Use a separate development org and the repository instructions to rehearse setup. If you cannot test a step, label it unverified and explain the dependency. A screenshot of a successful interface is useful, but it does not prove that a clean checkout can reproduce the project. Capture the actual test output and the commit it belongs to, without including credentials.

callouts.text: A public portfolio should contain work you are authorised to share and synthetic data. Do not copy private employer code into it.

sections.heading: Guide the reviewer through one important decision
body: Prepare a two-minute walkthrough: the user problem, the visible feature, one key implementation decision and the verification. Open the relevant code instead of browsing through every folder. Show a failure case as well as a successful request. For example, an unavailable vehicle should produce a useful error rather than a misleading success message.

Ask a peer to follow the README from a clean starting point. Record where they hesitate and improve those instructions. The aim is not to remove every question; good projects invite technical discussion. The aim is to make that discussion about your decisions and evidence rather than missing setup details.

callouts.text: A reviewer can identify the project’s context, reproduce a supported path and find the tests without asking you where to start.

exercise.title: Apply this to your own search
exercise.brief: Prepare one portfolio repository and rehearse a short review walkthrough.
steps: Write the README using the structure above.
Add a small diagram and a synthetic-data demonstration.
Review publishable files and repository history for private material.
Rehearse setup in a suitable development environment.
Ask a peer to review the README and record one improvement.
acceptance: Training context, ownership and limitations are explicit.
Setup and test instructions match the project.
The demonstration includes a success and a failure case.

knowledgeCheck.question: Does a screenshot prove reproducibility?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. It shows one observed state. Setup instructions and repeatable tests provide different evidence.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a design decision useful to a reviewer?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The requirement, chosen approach, alternative and trade-off are clear.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is one well-explained project often enough to begin?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It gives concrete material for a technical conversation; adding unexplained repositories does not automatically add evidence.

recap: Explain the project before the folders.
Demonstrate a decision and its limits.

illustration.prompt: Create one landscape 16:9 lesson-cover illustration for SAM Salesforce Developer Studio. Restrained professional editorial illustration, flat geometric drawn forms with fine navy linework and a subtle paper texture. Warm ivory #F7F4EE, navy #12253C, muted cobalt #3867E8, restrained teal #138A86 and sage. One clear central scene, generous empty margins, at most three main visual groups. Calm adult learning design. Any people are clearly drawn stylized figures, never realistic photos. NO text, letters, numerals, logos, watermarks, Salesforce mascots, decorative clutter or glossy 3D. Exact topic: Build a Portfolio. Subject: a small project display with an application, a simple architecture diagram and test evidence.
